intro: Ives’s Thoreau walks around Walden Pond, grows restless, then settles beside a repeated A–C–G in the piano’s bass. The Concord Sonata ends with delicate high chords and a question still hanging underneath.

sections.label: Intro · Rising chords in two keys
sections.mNote: Quiet piano figures climb through the opening

sections.label: A · Three walks from G major
sections.mNote: Each walk begins simply, quickens and subsides

sections.label: B · A–C–G repeats in the bass
sections.mNote: A freer melody wanders above the repeated notes

sections.label: C · Repeated chords grow insistent
sections.mNote: Dissonant piano chords gather into a sustained climax

sections.label: D · The bass figure comes back
sections.mNote: A–C–G returns before the opening figures stir again

sections.label: E · The sonata’s melody returns
sections.mNote: The recurring tune sounds above repeating piano figures

sections.label: Coda · High chords, a lower echo
sections.mNote: Delicate chords hang above an earlier phrase in the bass

cues.title: Two keys in the mist
cues.text: Quiet chords rise through the piano, sounding in two keys at once. Their little upward steps will return near the end. For now, each seems to appear through the haze and disappear again.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Thoreau”: rising opening figures and chords in two keys, later recalled. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An autumn day at Walden
cues.text: In his 1920 essay, Ives sets Thoreau beside Walden Pond on an autumn day: “a shadow of a thought at first, colored by the mist and haze over the pond”. The mist lifts; Thoreau grows restless and starts walking.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Thoreau”, paragraph beginning “And if there shall be a program”. Quotation retains Ives’s American spelling. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau

cues.title: Three walks from G major
cues.text: A plain G major chord starts the first of three walking episodes. Each quickens and grows louder before subsiding. The last builds towards a ringing, bell-like climax.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the three G major beginnings, accelerating walks and final bell-like climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three notes keep returning
cues.text: A–C–G rises from the bass, over and over. Above it a melody wanders in another key. The repeated notes let the piano keep moving while the tune takes its time.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the A–C–G ostinato after the walks and the independent upper melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chords become insistent
cues.text: The repeated piano chords grow tense and dissonant. Earlier in this stretch, a dotted rhythm has begun to reveal its kinship with the sonata’s recurring melody; now repetition drives the music towards a climax.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: dotted-rhythm figure related to the human-faith melody and the ensuing repetitive, dissonant climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A–C–G comes back
cues.text: The climax dies away in converging chords. The repeated bass figure and its wandering melody return, until figures from the opening page begin to stir the piano again.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: converging chords after the climax, return of the ostinato and melody, then introductory figures. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A symphony without Boston
cues.text: Thoreau plays the flute, but Ives is more interested in his ear. In the 1920 essay he writes that Thoreau “did not have to go to Boston to hear ‘the Symphony’”. There is music enough beside the pond.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), opening paragraph of “Thoreau”. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau

cues.title: The melody across four portraits
cues.text: The sonata’s recurring melody returns above repeating figures from this movement’s opening. Later the A–C–G pattern takes over beneath it. The tune that filled The Alcotts now sings inside a much quieter ending.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: cyclic melody over introductory figures, then the ostinato. Ives supplies a piano-only alternative to the flute version; this recording credits piano alone. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: High chords, an unanswered bass
cues.text: The opening figures return briefly, followed by delicate chords high on the piano. An earlier phrase sounds beneath them. The final notes keep a little dissonance: the sonata closes without the plain C major certainty of The Alcotts.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”, final paragraph: introductory recollection, high chords and lower earlier motive, ending with slight dissonance. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A G major chord starts the walk
transitions.from: Intro · Rising chords in two keys
transitions.to: A · Three walks from G major
transitions.how: The rising piano figures lead to a plain G major chord. It begins the first of three walking episodes, each growing quicker and louder before falling back. The same G major chord will start the next two attempts.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the introduction and the three walking episodes with G major beginnings. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The bass settles on three notes
transitions.from: A · Three walks from G major
transitions.to: B · A–C–G repeats in the bass
transitions.how: The last walk reaches a bell-like climax, then the piano begins repeating A–C–G in the bass. A melody in another key moves freely above it. The left hand keeps returning to the same three notes while the right hand wanders.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the end of the walks, A–C–G ostinato and independent upper melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The repeated chords grow harder
transitions.from: B · A–C–G repeats in the bass
transitions.how: The piano grows more animated, with a dotted-rhythm figure related to the sonata’s recurring melody. Repeated dissonant chords build towards a climax. The steady recurrence that first held the bass in place now makes the upper chords increasingly insistent.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the animated dotted-rhythm passage and later repetitive, dissonant climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Converging chords recover the bass figure
transitions.to: D · The bass figure comes back
transitions.how: The dissonant climax subsides in converging piano chords. A–C–G returns below the earlier wandering melody. Figures from the opening page then interrupt them and gradually grow more agitated.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: converging chords, return of the ostinato and melody, followed by the introductory figures. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The recurring melody sings above the piano
transitions.from: D · The bass figure comes back
transitions.how: The sonata’s recurring melody emerges above repeating figures from the introduction. As the melody continues, the accompaniment returns to A–C–G. The same tune now spans two of the movement’s most persistent piano patterns.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the cyclic melody over introductory figures and then the ostinato, with flute and piano-only versions. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: High chords above an earlier phrase
transitions.to: Coda · High chords, a lower echo
transitions.how: The recurring melody fades, leaving the piano’s repeated pattern. A brief return of the opening figures leads to delicate high chords, with an earlier phrase beneath them. The last notes retain a slight dissonance.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”, final paragraph: ostinato, introductory recollection, high chords and lower motive. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

composer.epithet: He sold life insurance in New York and wrote music in which a hymn across the river could outlast a whole marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut. Charles, born there in 1874, grew up with a father for whom a wrong note could be the beginning of an experiment.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, putting the tune of God Save the King through a teenager’s display of keyboard tricks. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and how to sustain a symphony. His First Symphony was the result: a young American speaking fluent European. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term. His son kept talking about him for the next sixty years.
